Another significant accomplishment was the development of methods to scale-up STRAP to recover ~kg quantities of resins from multilayer films, enabling the production of cast films using industrial equipment in partnership with Amcor. We tested three different methods to increase the scale of STRAP, each of which led to slightly different recovered resin properties. Our final approach, in which STRAP was performed using a heated jacketed dissolution vessel to maintain a high temperature during dissolution and filtration, led to high-quality films with mechanical properties similar to virgin resin (Sanchez-Rivera et al, ACS Mat Lett, 2025). These efforts were used to guide the design of a pilot-scale plant as an avenue for further analysis of STRAP scale-up, which is discussed in more detail in Section 5. An initially unanticipated challenge that was encountered and addressed during this award was the apparent yellow color of films cast from resins recovered during the application of STRAP to a reverse-printed multilayer film, even though the recovered STRAP resins appear white (like virgin resins). Yellow coloration decreases the value of recovered resins, motivating efforts to improve the optical properties of STRAP-based films. These efforts yielded several significant accomplishments. One accomplishment was the identification of the molecule responsible for the yellow color based on analyzing a panel of pigments as well as products of thermal decomposition. Upon identification of a decomposition product as the likely color source, we developed methods to combine mechanical filtration (to minimize solvent retention in the precipitated polymer) with the use of an adsorbent (to remove dissolved color bodies), leading to optically clear films (Yan et al, Sci Adv, 2025). Another accomplishment was the development of computational workflows to more generally determine solvents and operating conditions suitable for extracting contaminants, like soluble pigments, brominated flame retardants, and phthalates, during STRAP (Zhou et al, Green Chem, submitted). These new methods – both experimental and computational – can ensure the purity and high quality of STRAP-recovered resins and resulting films to facilitate commercial translation. Topic Area 6 – Educational and Outreach Activities in Plastic Recycling Public perception and knowledge of recycling technologies and plastics in general was a significant area of focus for CUWP. All of the feedstocks described here are obtained from consumers who chose to correctly recycle their plastic waste. This makes outreach pivotal for any organization reliant on sustainable feedstocks. As such courses centered around plastic recycling were developed and taught over the entire CUWP term at both the University of Wisconsin – Madison and Iowa State University. Through these courses students were able to visit local landfills, packaging companies, and film manufacturers. More easily digestible information sheets were also distributed to all collaborators or affiliates on topics such as the plastic supply chain and chemical recycling methods. Workshop programs for K-12 teachers were hosted showing hands-on classroom lessons based on STRAP for inclusion in teacher classrooms.
